title: Chocolate Mousse
subtitle: Dark chocolate and egg mousse, set in the fridge
excerpt: Dark chocolate melted and folded through whisked egg whites and yolks to make a rich, airy mousse. Set in the fridge for two hours. No cream, no gelatine.

recipe.sourceNotes: Chocolate mousse is a classic French dessert, with the first recorded recipe attributed to the painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, who was also an enthusiastic cook. The dish appeared in French cookbooks in the early 20th century and became a restaurant staple. The authentic French version uses no cream; the airy texture comes entirely from whisked egg whites. The eggs are separated, the yolks whisked into the chocolate for richness, and the egg whites whisked to stiff peaks and folded in for lightness. The result is a mousse that is simultaneously intense and light. Some British versions add cream, which makes a richer but heavier result.

content.text: The chocolate must be fully melted and cooled to room temperature before the eggs are added, or they will scramble. Whisk the egg whites in a clean, dry bowl: any trace of fat or moisture will prevent them from forming stiff peaks. Fold the egg whites in in two additions: the first to loosen the chocolate mixture, the second very gently to preserve the air.
Melt the chocolate and butter in a bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water. Stir until smooth. Remove and leave to cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk the egg yolks and 20 g of the caster sugar together until pale and slightly thick. Stir into the cooled chocolate with the vanilla.
In a clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with the pinch of salt to soft peaks. Add the remaining 20 g sugar and whisk to stiff, glossy peaks.

Stir a large spoonful of egg white into the chocolate to loosen it. Gently fold in the rest in two more additions, cutting and folding rather than stirring. Divide between glasses or ramekins. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
